topic: DP-3T: The Privacy-First Way to Trace Contacts

sections.title: The Privacy Dilemma: Centralized vs. Decentralized
sections.content: Introduce the challenge of contact tracing during a pandemic. Contrast a 'Big Brother' model (Centralized) where a server tracks everyone's location, with the 'Privacy-First' model (DP-3T) where users keep their own logs. Define DP-3T: Decentralized Privacy-Preserving Proximity Tracing.
sections.example: Imagine Alice and Bob are in a park. In a centralized system, a 'Spy' records their meeting. In DP-3T, Alice and Bob exchange 'secret handshakes' that only they know, and no one else is watching.

sections.title: Prerequisite: One-Way Hash Functions & PRFs
sections.content: Explain the building blocks: 1. Cryptographic Hash Functions (y = H(x)) - easy to calculate, impossible to reverse. 2. Pseudo-Random Functions (PRF). Use a graphical 'Meat Grinder' metaphor to show data going in and a unique, irreversible string coming out.
sections.example: Visual: Input 'Apple' -> Meat Grinder -> 'x89k2...'. You can't turn 'x89k2...' back into 'Apple'. This ensures that even if an ID is stolen, the user's identity remains hidden.

sections.title: Step 1: Generating Daily Keys and Ephemeral IDs (EphID)
sections.content: Explain the key hierarchy. Every day, the phone generates a 'Secret Day Key' (SK_t). From this key, it derives multiple 'Ephemeral IDs' (EphIDs) that change every 15 minutes to prevent tracking over time. Use a tree diagram to show the derivation.
sections.example: Alice's phone creates a Master Key for Monday. From this, it spawns 'EphID_1' at 9:00 AM and 'EphID_2' at 9:15 AM. To a bystander, 'EphID_1' and 'EphID_2' look like they belong to completely different people.

sections.title: Step 2: The Bluetooth Handshake (Broadcasting)
sections.content: Describe how phones use Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE). Alice's phone broadcasts her current EphID while simultaneously listening for others. When Bob is near Alice, they exchange and store each other's EphIDs locally on their phones, along with the date and signal strength.
sections.example: Alice's phone shouts 'Code Red!' (EphID_A). Bob's phone hears it and writes it in a private notebook. Bob's phone shouts 'Code Blue!' (EphID_B). Alice writes it down. Neither knows the other's real name.

sections.title: Step 3: Reporting a Positive Case
sections.content: When Alice tests positive, she voluntarily uploads her 'Secret Day Key' (SK_t) for the period she was infectious to a central server. Crucially, she does NOT upload her contact list or her personal identity.
sections.example: Alice sends her 'Monday Master Key' to the public bulletin board. The board now lists: 'Someone who had this key is sick,' but it doesn't say it was Alice.

sections.title: Step 4: Local Matching and Notification
sections.content: Every user (like Bob) periodically downloads the list of 'Sick Day Keys' from the server. Bob’s phone uses these keys to re-generate the EphIDs that the sick person would have broadcasted. If any of those match the IDs in Bob's local notebook, Bob gets an alert.
sections.example: Bob's phone takes the 'Monday Master Key' from the server, runs it through the 'Meat Grinder' (PRF) to get 'EphID_1', 'EphID_2', etc. It sees 'EphID_1' matches his notebook entry. Bob's phone vibrates: 'You were near a positive case!'

sections.title: Summary: Why It Works
sections.content: Recap the 'Decentralized' nature: The server never knows who met whom. It only distributes keys. Privacy is maintained because IDs are temporary, and matching happens locally on the user's device.
sections.example: Visual recap: A 5-step loop showing Alice/Bob -> ID exchange -> Alice sick -> Key upload -> Bob's local match. Conclusion: Technology protecting health without sacrificing liberty.
